extraction.name: PIQA: Physical Interaction Question Answering
extraction.description: PIQA is a benchmark dataset for evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding systems. The dataset consists of multiple choice question answering pairs where a model must choose the most appropriate solution to a physical goal from two options. It contains over 16,000 training QA pairs with an additional 2K and 3K held out for development and testing respectively. The dataset is inspired by instructables.com and focuses on everyday situations with a preference for atypical solutions.
extraction.creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi
extraction.publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI)
extraction.citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., and Choi, Y. (2020). PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. AAAI 2020.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected using Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) annotators who were prompted with links to instructables.com. Annotators were asked to glance at the instructions of an instructable and construct two component tasks, articulate a physical goal and a valid solution, and provide a permutation (trick) to their own solution which makes it invalid. Annotators were seeded with instructables drawn from six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop. Two examples were drawn per instructable. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. This often meant that correct examples were removed that required expert level knowledge of a domain (e.g. special woodworking terminology) which should not fall under the umbrella of commonsense.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Instructions from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for doing everything from cooking to car repair. Annotators used these as inspiration to construct goal-solution pairs.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The AFLite algorithm was used to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples from the data. AFLite performs systematic data bias reduction by discarding instances whose given feature representations are collectively highly indicative of the target label. 5,000 examples from the original dataset were used to fine-tune BERT-Large and compute embeddings of all remaining instances. AFLite uses an ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets of the data to determine whether pre-computed embeddings are strong indicators of the correct answer option.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Data was tokenized using Spacy. The AFLite algorithm was applied to remove annotation artifacts and spurious biases. Train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite. Examples with low annotator agreement were removed during validation. The GPT BPE tokenizer was used for sequence length analysis, with the longest 1% of data removed for that analysis.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were provided prompts derived from instructables.com. They were asked to: (1) provide a physical goal often centered on atypical materials, (2) provide a valid solution for achieving the goal, and (3) provide a trick - a permutation of their solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong, often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. A qualification HIT was run prior to the main annotation stage where annotators had to successfully identify (>80%) well-formed and underspecified goal-solution pairs. Data was collected in batches and validated by other annotators for correctness. Users with low agreement were de-qualified. An interface with a diff button was included to highlight where solutions differ.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Examples with low agreement were removed from the data during validation. Human performance was calculated by majority vote. Annotators chosen for human performance evaluation achieved 90% on the qualification HIT. Annotator pay averaged >$15/hr according to both self-reporting on turkerview.com and timing calculations.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Spacy (tokenization), AFLite algorithm (bias reduction using BERT-Large embeddings and ensemble of linear classifiers)
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance AI systems' understanding of physical commonsense knowledge, which is critical for day-to-day human life including problem solving and expressing needs and desires. The research aims to build language representations useful beyond the NLP community, including for robots that interact with the world and understand natural language.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset was constructed to be adversarial to BERT. Reporting bias was identified as a challenge during data collection, where annotators tended toward prototypical solutions and common tools. AFLite was applied to reduce annotation artifacts. The dataset was specifically designed to flatten the distribution of referenced objects to counteract reporting bias.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Large pretrained models struggle with the dataset (~77% accuracy vs 95% human accuracy). The dataset focuses on English only. Models pretrained on large web crawls may eventually surpass human performance by finding large sources of in-domain data, but this does not address the underlying limitation of learning physical knowledge from language alone. The dataset may not capture all dimensions of physical commonsense knowledge.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for benchmarking progress in physical commonsense understanding, evaluating language representations on their knowledge of physical commonsense, and as a diagnostic tool for probing the physical understanding of deep pretrained language models. It can be used for training, validation, and testing of natural language understanding models.
